chunks.text: Casuarina equisetifolia, described by Linnaeus in 1759, belongs to its own family, Casuarinaceae, and despite its pine-like appearance is a flowering plant, not a conifer. Two subspecies are recognised: equisetifolia (taller, 7–35 m) and incana (shorter, 6–12 m). The species name 'equisetifolia' refers to its horsetail-like, needle-fine foliage. It is native across a wide Indo-Pacific range — India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and parts of Australia (Queensland, New South Wales, Northern Territory) — and has since been introduced very widely elsewhere. It is evergreen and monoecious, with drooping branchlets of tiny scale-like leaves in whorls of 7–8, separate male and female catkin-like flower clusters on the same tree, small woody cone-like fruiting structures 10–24 mm across that release winged seeds, and bark that is smooth and grey when young, becoming scaly and greyish-brown to black with age.

It is widely planted in dense rows as a coastal windbreak and to stabilise sandy soil against erosion, and is considered a suitable species for reclaiming degraded wasteland in India. Its wood is used as fuelwood and for pulp rather than fine furniture. As a nitrogen-fixing actinorhizal plant, its roots host Frankia bacteria in root nodules, which naturally enriches the surrounding soil — a genuine ecological benefit, though the species has also become invasive outside its native range in places such as the United States and South Africa, where biological control insects have been used to manage it. It is rated Least Concern by the IUCN. In the Philippines, the town of Agoo takes its name from the local word for this tree.
